# Define the subset

One of the aspects noticed during analysis is the percentage of individuals that never graduated college that also had meaningful employment in the region. The table below shows that 58% of the high school graduates in Northeast Minnesota never graduated college.

```{r}
data <- master.original %>%
  filter(ps.grad != "Attending ps") %>%
  group_by(ps.grad) %>%
  summarize(n = n()) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(pct = n / sum(n))

datatable(data, class = "cell-border stripe", filter = "top", rownames = FALSE,
          options = list(columnDefs = list(list(className = "dt-center", targets = 1:2)))) %>%
  formatCurrency(2, "", digits = 0) %>%
  formatPercentage(3, digits = 1)


```

We are going to examine, more closely, this 58% of the population and see if there are patterns in which they end up in different employment outcomes 1-, 5- and 10-years after graduating high school.

<br>

# Employment outcomes distribution

The following tables provide the percentage of non-college graduates that were categorized in the various employment outcomes at 1-, 5-, and 10-years after graduating high school.

**Key Findings**\
At Year 1, most non-graduates were concentrated in non-meaningful employment (35.0%) or had no Minnesota employment record (20.8%). Meaningful regional employment accounted for 19.2%, while meaningful employment elsewhere in Minnesota was minimal (5.6%). By Year 5, regional meaningful employment rose to 26.3% and became the largest single category, non-meaningful work declined to 27.3%, and meaningful employment outside the region more than doubled to 12.6%. By Year 10, regional meaningful employment held steady at 25.6% and meaningful employment outside the region grew slightly to 15.6%, but detachment from the state labor market surged to 36.7%.

**Interpretation Over Time**\
Year 1 reflects a difficult transition for non-graduates, with most in unstable or disconnected positions. By Year 5, there is clear upward mobility as regional meaningful employment strengthens and non-meaningful work declines. This marks the high point of progress for those remaining in the workforce. However, by Year 10 the picture stabilizes, with little additional growth in meaningful employment. Instead, labor market detachment grows substantially, overtaking all other categories and becoming the dominant outcome.

**Conclusion**\
Non-graduates make early gains toward meaningful regional employment, particularly within the first five years, but these gains plateau by Year 10. The growing share with no Minnesota employment record highlights long-term fragility in workforce attachment, suggesting that without intervention, a significant portion of this group will remain disconnected from the state’s labor market.

::: panel-tabset
## 1 year after graduation

Most non-graduates did not secure meaningful employment early on. Over one-third (35.0%) were employed in Minnesota but not in meaningful work, while another 20.8% had no Minnesota employment record and were not in school. Meaningful employment in the region (19.2%) was far more common than meaningful employment elsewhere in Minnesota (5.6%). A notable share (19.4%) continued their postsecondary education despite not completing a credential.

```{r}
data <- master.original %>%
  filter(ps.grad == "No") %>%
  filter(grad.year.1 != "After 2023") %>%
  group_by(grad.year.1) %>%
  summarize(n = n()) %>%
  ungroup %>%
  mutate(pct = n / sum(n))

datatable(data, class = "cell-border stripe", filter = "top", rownames = FALSE,
          options = list(columnDefs = list(list(className = "dt-center", targets = 1:2)))) %>%
  formatCurrency(2, "", digits = 0) %>%
  formatPercentage(3, digits = 1)
```

## 5 years after graduation

The share of individuals in postsecondary dropped sharply (19.4% → 4.2%), reflecting that most either left school or completed without graduating. Meaningful employment in the region grew steadily (19.2% → 26.3%), signaling that the region became a stronger employment destination over time. Meaningful employment outside the region also more than doubled (5.6% → 12.6%), though it remained less common than regional pathways. Non-meaningful employment declined (35.0% → 27.3%), but the proportion with no Minnesota employment record stayed high (20.8% → 29.6%), suggesting long-term detachment from the state labor force for a sizeable share.

```{r}
data <- master.original %>%
  filter(ps.grad == "No") %>%
  filter(grad.year.5 != "After 2023") %>%
  group_by(grad.year.5) %>%
  summarize(n = n()) %>%
  ungroup %>%
  mutate(pct = n / sum(n))

datatable(data, class = "cell-border stripe", filter = "top", rownames = FALSE,
          options = list(columnDefs = list(list(className = "dt-center", targets = 1:2)))) %>%
  formatCurrency(2, "", digits = 0) %>%
  formatPercentage(3, digits = 1)
```

## 10 years after graduation

Meaningful regional employment held steady (26.3% → 25.6%), suggesting limited additional gains after the first five years. Meaningful employment elsewhere in Minnesota declined (12.6% → 15.6%), indicating a modest shift outward from the region. Non-meaningful employment fell again (27.3% → 22.1%), pointing to some continued upward mobility. However, the most striking change was in detachment: those with no Minnesota employment record jumped from 29.6% to 36.7%, showing that long-term disconnection from the state labor market becomes the dominant outcome by Year 10.

```{r}
data <- master.original %>%
  filter(ps.grad == "No") %>%
  filter(grad.year.10 != "After 2023") %>%
  group_by(grad.year.10) %>%
  summarize(n = n()) %>%
  ungroup %>%
  mutate(pct = n / sum(n))

datatable(data, class = "cell-border stripe", filter = "top", rownames = FALSE,
          options = list(columnDefs = list(list(className = "dt-center", targets = 1:2)))) %>%
  formatCurrency(2, "", digits = 0) %>%
  formatPercentage(3, digits = 1)

```
:::

This analysis is going to focus on that 58% of the graduates, and explore relationships and patterns of the portion of this population that found meaningful employment in the region vs. other employment outcomes.

<br>

# Methodology

The above tables show the importance of understanding how non-college grads are navigating their post-high school pathways with a significant portion of them being disconnected from the regional workforce. To better understand these pathways, we will explore the relationships between independent variables (Demographic, High school characteristics, and High school accomplishments) along with workforce outcomes at 1-, 5- and 10-years after graduating high school.

Since we provided the descriptive statistics above, we now need to analyze which factors relate most strongly to outcomes, and then see if we can use those factors to build a predictive model.

For exploring the relationships we will do the following;

-   For **categorical predictors** (e.g., Race/Ethnicity, Economic status, CTE achievement, PSEO participation), use cross-tabs with Cramer’s V and chi-square.
-   For **continuous predictors** (e.g., ACT, MCA scores, total CTE courses, county-level variables), use ANOVA to compare means across the employment states.
-   Run these analyses separately for grad.year.1, grad.year.5, grad.year.10 to see how relationships shift over time.

For building the predictive model, we will do the following;

-   Identify important predictors
    -   Focus on effect sizes rather than just significance (since large N will make almost everything significant).
    -   Highlight **which variables consistently show moderate-to-strong associations** with employment outcomes.
    -   These become the candidates for inclusion in CART modeling.
-   For each year (1, 5, 10), run CART where the dependent variable is a **binary comparison with “Meaningful emp region”** as the reference:
    -   Meaningful emp region vs. Meaningful emp MN
    -   Meaningful emp region vs. Not meaningful, not attending ps
    -   Meaningful emp region vs. No MN emp record, not attending ps

This will:

-   Show **which factors distinguish students who stay employed meaningfully in their region** from those in other outcomes.
-   Provide **clear decision rules** (e.g., *“Non-college grads with high ACT scores and PSEO experience are far more likely to achieve meaningful regional employment.”*).
-   Feed directly into actionable insights for policymakers.

<br>

# Independent variables

We are going to continue using the variables that we have used throughout this project.

-   **Demographic:** `RaceEthnicity`, `economic.status`, `SpecialEdStatus`
-   **High school characteristics:** `Dem_Desc`, `avg.unemp.rate`, `avg.wages.pct.state`
-   **High school accomplishments:** `pseo.participant`, `cte.achievement`, `total.cte.courses.taken`, `ACTCompositeScore`, `took.ACT`, `MCA.M`, `MCA.R`, `MCA.S`

<br>

# Relationships

We will first explore the relationships between the independent variables and the 1-, 5- and 10-year outcomes.

## Demographics

**Key Findings**\
Among demographic variables, the strength of association with employment outcomes for non-college graduates ranges from weak to moderate. The relative influence is:

1.  **Special Education Status** – strongest predictor, with moderate effects (Cramer’s V ≈ 0.10–0.16), consistently linked to lower meaningful regional employment and higher disconnection.
2.  **Economic Status** – moderate influence (Cramer’s V ≈ 0.08–0.10), shaping job quality and access to meaningful regional employment, though less predictive of long-term detachment.
3.  **Race/Ethnicity** – weakest but still significant (Cramer’s V ≈ 0.05–0.06), highlighting disparities in meaningful regional employment and long-term workforce attachment.

**Interpretation Over Time**

-   **Year 1:** Disparities emerge immediately. Students of color (especially Black, Hispanic, and Asian/PI) and those with special education status face lower rates of meaningful regional employment and higher rates of detachment or non-meaningful work. Low-income students are more likely to be in non-meaningful jobs but show similar regional meaningful employment rates to their peers.
-   **Year 5:** Regional meaningful employment grows across groups, but gaps persist. Special education students remain more likely to be disconnected or in non-meaningful roles. Race/Ethnicity disparities widen as White and American Indian students gain stronger footholds in regional employment while Black, Hispanic, and Asian/PI students face higher disconnection. Economic status differences become more evident in job quality, with low-income students lagging.
-   **Year 10:** Patterns stabilize into long-term trajectories. Special education status remains the most consistent barrier to meaningful regional employment. Race/Ethnicity disparities deepen, with workforce detachment affecting more than half of Asian/PI and Hispanic students compared to about one-third of White students. Economic status continues to shape job quality, though disconnection rates converge across income levels.

**Conclusion**\
Demographic characteristics meaningfully influence non-college graduates’ pathways into the workforce, with special education status standing out as the strongest and most consistent predictor of disadvantage. Race/Ethnicity disparities reveal systemic inequities, particularly in long-term workforce attachment for students of color, while economic status most strongly impacts job quality. Together, these findings show that while demographic effects are not the sole drivers of employment outcomes, they create enduring barriers that limit equitable access to meaningful regional employment.

<br>

### `RaceEthnicity`

**Key Findings**\
Across Years 1, 5, and 10, Race/Ethnicity consistently shows a statistically significant relationship with employment outcomes, though effect sizes remain weak (Cramer’s V = 0.047–0.063). White and American Indian students are consistently more likely to secure meaningful employment in the region (ranging from 17–27%), while Black, Hispanic, and Asian/PI students remain less represented in these jobs (typically 10–17%). Disconnection from the Minnesota labor market is persistently higher for Asian/PI and Hispanic students, climbing to more than half of each group by Year 10, compared with roughly one-third of White peers.

**Interpretation Over Time**

-   **Year 1:** Disparities emerge immediately, with White and American Indian students more likely to access meaningful regional jobs, while Black, Hispanic, and Asian/PI peers experience higher rates of non-meaningful employment or detachment.
-   **Year 5:** Meaningful regional employment rises across all groups, but gaps persist. Disconnection begins to sharply diverge for Asian/PI and Hispanic students, who are increasingly disconnected compared to White peers.
-   **Year 10:** Patterns solidify. White and American Indian students sustain stronger representation in meaningful regional employment, while long-term detachment dominates for Asian/PI and Hispanic students, with nearly half or more disconnected from the state’s workforce.

**Conclusion**\
While the overall statistical association between Race/Ethnicity and employment outcomes is modest, the persistence of disparities is clear. White and American Indian non-graduates are better integrated into meaningful regional employment, while Black, Hispanic, and Asian/PI peers face enduring barriers and disproportionately higher rates of workforce disconnection. These results highlight systemic inequities in labor market access and underscore the need for targeted interventions to support underrepresented groups in achieving and sustaining meaningful regional employment.

::: panel-tabset
#### 1-year after graduation

**Key Findings**\
At Year 1, Race/Ethnicity shows a statistically significant relationship with employment outcomes (χ²=188.6, p\<.001), though the effect size is weak (Cramer’s V=0.047). White and American Indian students had the highest rates of meaningful regional employment (19.2% and 17.4%), while Black (11.7%), Hispanic (11.6%), and Asian/PI (10.0%) students were less likely to be employed meaningfully in the region. Non-meaningful employment was the most common outcome across all groups, with disconnection from Minnesota’s workforce particularly high among Asian/PI (35.0%) and Hispanic (32.5%) students.

**Interpretation**\
The data suggest that in the first year after graduation, non-college graduates from underrepresented racial/ethnic groups are less likely to secure meaningful employment in the region compared to White or American Indian peers. Instead, they face higher rates of disconnection or concentration in non-meaningful employment. This points to early disparities in how different groups connect to the regional labor market, with meaningful regional employment disproportionately concentrated among White and American Indian students.

**Conclusion**\
While the overall effect of Race/Ethnicity is weak, the disparities are clear: Black, Hispanic, and Asian/PI non-graduates are less likely to enter meaningful regional employment in the critical first year. These patterns highlight structural barriers that may hinder equitable access to quality regional jobs and suggest the need for targeted supports to improve early labor market attachment for underrepresented groups.

```{r}
data <- master.original %>%
  filter(grad.year.1 != "After 2023") %>%
  filter(ps.grad == "No") %>%
  filter(RaceEthnicity != "Unknown")

tab_xtab(var.row = data$grad.year.1,
         var.col = data$RaceEthnicity,
         show.exp = TRUE,
         show.col.prc = TRUE)

```

#### 5-years after graduation

**Key Findings**\
At Year 5, Race/Ethnicity remains statistically significant in predicting employment outcomes (χ²=188.0, p\<.001), though the effect size is weak (Cramer’s V=0.052). White students continued to have the highest share of meaningful regional employment (27.3%), followed by American Indian students (23.0%). In contrast, Black (15.0%), Hispanic (16.9%), and Asian/PI (17.9%) students were less likely to secure meaningful employment in the region. Disconnection from the Minnesota labor market was especially high among Asian/PI (45.9%) and Hispanic (47.7%) students compared to 28.9% of White students.

**Interpretation**\
By Year 5, regional meaningful employment increased across all groups, but disparities persisted. White and American Indian non-graduates were most likely to benefit from meaningful regional jobs, while Black, Hispanic, and Asian/PI peers remained underrepresented in these opportunities. Importantly, workforce detachment became a more pronounced issue for Asian/PI and Hispanic students, who were disproportionately disconnected from the state’s employment system.

**Conclusion**\
The Year 5 outcomes show that while regional meaningful employment grows overall, racial/ethnic disparities continue to shape labor market experiences. White and American Indian students have stronger footholds in the regional workforce, while Black, Hispanic, and Asian/PI students face both lower regional employment rates and higher disconnection. This suggests that structural inequalities established in the early years persist and deepen, limiting equitable access to meaningful regional employment for underrepresented groups.

```{r}
data <- master.original %>%
  filter(grad.year.5 != "After 2023") %>%
  filter(ps.grad == "No") %>%
  filter(RaceEthnicity != "Unknown")

tab_xtab(var.row = data$grad.year.5,
         var.col = data$RaceEthnicity,
         show.exp = TRUE,
         show.col.prc = TRUE)
```

#### 10-years after graduation

**Key Findings**\
At Year 10, Race/Ethnicity continues to show a statistically significant relationship with employment outcomes (χ²=120.3, p\<.001), though the effect size remains weak (Cramer’s V=0.063). White students had the highest share of meaningful regional employment (26.5%), followed by American Indian students (23.8%). Black (12.0%), Hispanic (14.6%), and Asian/PI (10.8%) students were far less likely to achieve meaningful regional employment. Workforce detachment became a dominant outcome, especially among Asian/PI (58.1%) and Hispanic (51.1%) students, compared to 36.0% of White students.

**Interpretation**\
By Year 10, disparities in labor market outcomes persist and in some cases widen. White and American Indian students maintain stronger footholds in regional meaningful employment, while Black, Hispanic, and Asian/PI students remain disproportionately excluded. The most striking difference lies in long-term detachment: over half of Asian/PI and Hispanic non-graduates are disconnected from the state workforce, a rate far higher than for White or American Indian peers.

**Conclusion**\
The Year 10 outcomes highlight enduring structural inequities in the regional labor market. While a subset of White and American Indian students sustain meaningful employment in the region, Black, Hispanic, and Asian/PI students face compounded barriers, with disconnection from the workforce emerging as the dominant trajectory. These long-term gaps underscore the importance of targeted strategies to improve retention and advancement in meaningful regional employment for underrepresented racial/ethnic groups.

```{r}
data <- master.original %>%
  filter(grad.year.10 != "After 2023") %>%
  filter(ps.grad == "No") %>%
  filter(RaceEthnicity != "Unknown")

tab_xtab(var.row = data$grad.year.10,
         var.col = data$RaceEthnicity,
         show.exp = TRUE,
         show.col.prc = TRUE)
```
:::

<br>

### `economic.status`

**Key Findings**\
Across Years 1, 5, and 10, economic status consistently shows a statistically significant relationship with employment outcomes, with small but persistent effects (Cramer’s V = 0.076–0.097). The strongest differences appear in job quality: non-low-income students are more likely to secure meaningful regional employment (24–28%) and less likely to be in non-meaningful jobs (19–32%), while low-income students face higher rates of non-meaningful work. Workforce detachment rates are similar for both groups at each time point.

**Interpretation Over Time**

-   **Year 1:** Differences are visible mainly in postsecondary continuation and non-meaningful employment, with low-income students less likely to be in school and more likely to work in non-meaningful jobs. Regional meaningful employment rates were nearly identical across groups.
-   **Year 5:** Gaps widen in job quality. Non-low-income students are more likely to move into meaningful regional employment (28.1% vs. 24.5%), while low-income students remain more concentrated in non-meaningful work. Disconnection levels are nearly the same across groups.
-   **Year 10:** Patterns persist. Non-low-income students sustain higher regional meaningful employment (27.8% vs. 23.1%) and lower non-meaningful employment (19.3% vs. 25.3%). Both groups experience high and nearly identical levels of workforce detachment (36–37%).

**Conclusion**\
Economic status matters less for whether non-college graduates remain connected to the Minnesota workforce and more for the type of jobs they hold. Low-income students are consistently less likely to attain meaningful regional employment and more likely to be in non-meaningful roles, while disconnection rates remain high and similar across groups. This suggests that long-term workforce participation challenges are broadly shared, but economic disadvantage creates enduring barriers to accessing quality regional employment.

::: panel-tabset

Rates of meaningful regional employment were nearly identical (19.1% vs. 19.3%), showing that early disparities are driven more by school continuation and job quality than by access to regional meaningful work.

### `SpecialEdStatus`

**Key Findings**\
Across Years 1, 5, and 10, special education status consistently shows a significant relationship with employment outcomes, with small-to-moderate effects (Cramer’s V = 0.097–0.157). Students without special education services are more likely to secure meaningful regional employment (20–27%) and meaningful employment elsewhere in Minnesota (14–17%), while students with special education status consistently lag behind (15–22% regional, 9–10% elsewhere). Those with special education status are also more likely to be disconnected or in non-meaningful work at every time point.

**Interpretation Over Time**

-   **Year 1:** Early disparities emerge sharply. Students with special education status are less likely to be in postsecondary or meaningful regional employment and more likely to be disconnected (29.5% vs. 18.0%) or in non-meaningful jobs (38.2% vs. 33.9%).
-   **Year 5:** Regional meaningful employment rises for both groups, but gaps persist (27.4% vs. 22.5%). Special education students remain more concentrated in disconnection (34.4% vs. 28.2%) and non-meaningful work (30.8% vs. 26.2%).
-   **Year 10:** Differences stabilize into long-term patterns. Non-special education students sustain stronger meaningful regional employment (26.6% vs. 22.0%), while special education students remain more likely to be disconnected (39.7% vs. 35.9%) or in non-meaningful jobs (27.9% vs. 20.5%).

**Conclusion**\
Special education status is one of the strongest demographic predictors of employment outcomes for non-college graduates. While both groups face high disconnection rates over time, students with special education status are consistently less likely to secure meaningful regional employment and more likely to be detached from the workforce or in non-meaningful roles. These persistent gaps highlight the need for tailored supports to improve workforce integration and long-term job quality for this population.

Students with special education status were far more likely to be disconnected (29.5% vs. 18.0%) or in non-meaningful jobs (38.2% vs. 33.9%), underscoring early disadvantages in workforce integration.

## High school characteristics

**Key Findings**\
Among High School Characteristics, the strength of association with non-college graduate outcomes ranges from weak to moderate. The relative influence is:

1.  **County Unemployment Rate** – strongest predictor (F=52.1 → 7.1), consistently linked to lower meaningful regional employment and higher detachment in higher-unemployment counties.
2.  **County Wages (% of State)** – moderate predictor (F=14.5 → 6.5), with students from higher-wage counties more likely to stay in their home region for meaningful work.
3.  **Rural-ness (Dem_Desc)** – weakest predictor (Cramer’s V ≈ 0.03–0.06), showing that students from entirely rural counties are less likely to achieve meaningful regional employment and more likely to seek work outside their region.

**Interpretation Over Time**

-   **Year 1:** County economic conditions strongly shaped early pathways. Students from stronger local economies (lower unemployment, higher wages) were more likely to secure meaningful regional jobs, while those from rural or weaker economies faced disadvantages.
-   **Year 5:** The influence of county unemployment and wages remained significant, though weaker. Students from healthier economies stayed in their region for meaningful work, while those from high-unemployment counties were more likely to disconnect or seek work elsewhere. Rural disadvantages became clearer, with entirely rural students showing the lowest regional employment rates.
-   **Year 10:** Effects of local conditions persisted but narrowed. County unemployment and wages still tilted outcomes toward meaningful regional work, though less strongly. Rural students continued to lag in meaningful regional employment, often relying on jobs outside their region.

**Conclusion**\
High School Characteristics matter most in the early years, when local labor market conditions at the time of graduation heavily shape pathways into meaningful regional employment. Over time, their influence weakens but does not disappear. Students from stronger county economies (low unemployment, higher wages) consistently fare better, while entirely rural students face persistent barriers to securing meaningful employment within their home regions.

<br>

### `Dem_Desc`

**Key Findings**\
Rural-ness shows a consistent, statistically significant relationship with outcomes for non-college graduates, though the effects are weak (Cramer’s V ≈ 0.03–0.06). Within the High School Characteristics group, it is among the weaker predictors. The relative outcomes are clear:

-   **Urban/town/rural mix** – consistently highest regional meaningful employment (20–27%).
-   **Town/rural mix** – mid-range outcomes (18–24%).
-   **Entirely rural** – lowest regional meaningful employment (15–21%) but highest meaningful employment outside the region (20–24%).

**Interpretation Over Time**

-   **Year 1:** Urban/town/rural mix students had the strongest foothold in meaningful regional employment (19.6%), while entirely rural students lagged (15.6%) and leaned more heavily on non-meaningful jobs.
-   **Year 5:** Gaps widened. Urban/town/rural mix students reached 27.6% in regional meaningful employment, compared to 24.0% for town/rural mix and only 21.0% for entirely rural students. Entirely rural students had the highest rates of meaningful employment outside the region (20.0%), suggesting limited local options.
-   **Year 10:** Patterns stabilized. Urban/town/rural mix students maintained the advantage in regional meaningful work (26.9%), while entirely rural peers remained lowest (20.0%) and continued to rely more on jobs outside the region (24.0%). Detachment rates converged across all groups at around 36%.

**Conclusion**\
Rural-ness modestly influences non-college graduates’ employment pathways. Students from entirely rural areas are less likely to achieve meaningful employment in their home region and more likely to find meaningful work elsewhere in Minnesota. By contrast, students from more mixed urban/rural backgrounds consistently achieve higher rates of meaningful regional employment. This suggests that geographic context shapes opportunity structures, with rural students facing persistent barriers to staying meaningfully employed within their region.

Urban/town/rural mix students had slightly higher meaningful regional employment (19.6%) compared to town/rural mix (18.8%) and entirely rural (15.6%). Entirely rural students had the lowest regional employment rates and slightly higher reliance on non-meaningful jobs, indicating modest early disadvantages.

### `avg.unemp.rate`

**Key Findings**\
County unemployment rate shows a consistent, statistically significant relationship with outcomes across all three years, though its influence weakens over time (F=52.1 → 16.8 → 7.1). Students with meaningful regional employment consistently came from counties with lower unemployment compared to peers in other categories, highlighting the importance of local economic health in shaping access to quality jobs.

**Interpretation Over Time**

-   **Year 1:** Students in meaningful regional employment came from counties with unemployment rates about 0.1–0.4 points lower than peers attending postsecondary, disconnected, or in non-meaningful jobs. Strong local economies supported immediate entry into meaningful regional work.\
-   **Year 5:** Gaps narrowed but remained significant. Regional workers came from counties with unemployment rates about 0.2 points lower than those attending postsecondary, disconnected, or working meaningfully outside the region, showing county conditions still influenced mid-term pathways.\
-   **Year 10:** The effect weakened but persisted. Regional workers came from counties with unemployment rates about 0.15 points lower than peers in meaningful jobs elsewhere in Minnesota or disconnected, suggesting local economic health still matters for retaining workers in the region.

**Conclusion**\
County unemployment rate is one of the stronger High School Characteristics predictors of meaningful regional employment, especially in the early years after graduation. While its influence declines over time, students from stronger county economies are consistently more likely to secure and remain in meaningful regional jobs.

::: panel-tabset
#### 1-year after graduation

**Key Takeaways (Year 1, County Unemployment Rate)**\
County unemployment rate is strongly related to outcomes (F=52.1, p\<.001). Students with meaningful regional employment tended to come from counties with lower unemployment compared to peers in other outcomes. This suggests that stronger local economies provide more direct opportunities for meaningful regional work in the first year after graduation.

**Significant Comparisons and Interpretation of "Diff"**

-   **Meaningful regional employment vs. Attending PS**
    -   Diff = **-0.39**, p \< .001
    -   Regional workers came from counties with unemployment rates about 0.4 points lower than those attending postsecondary.
    -   Interpretation: Students in stronger labor markets were more likely to go directly into regional employment rather than continue schooling.
-   **Meaningful regional employment vs. No MN employment record**
    -   Diff = **-0.11**, p = .002
    -   Regional workers came from counties with unemployment rates 0.1 points lower than disconnected peers.
    -   Interpretation: Even modestly lower unemployment reduced the risk of being detached from the workforce.
-   **Meaningful regional employment vs. Not meaningful employment**
    -   Diff = **-0.10**, p = .002
    -   Regional workers came from counties with unemployment rates 0.1 points lower than non-meaningfully employed peers.
    -   Interpretation: Lower county unemployment tilted outcomes toward meaningful rather than low-quality work.
-   **Other comparisons** (e.g., disconnection vs. non-meaningful work) were not significant, showing those groups had similar unemployment conditions.

```{r}
data <- master.original %>%
  filter(grad.year.1 != "After 2023") %>%
  filter(ps.grad == "No")

summary <- aov(avg.unemp.rate ~ grad.year.1, data = data)

summary

anova_df <- broom::tidy(summary)

TukeyHSD(summary)

tukey_df <- broom::tidy(TukeyHSD(summary))

wb <- createWorkbook()
addWorksheet(wb, "ANOVA")
addWorksheet(wb, "TukeyHSD")
writeData(wb, "ANOVA", anova_df)
writeData(wb, "TukeyHSD", tukey_df)
saveWorkbook(wb, "Data/ChatGPT/Non-college grads/High school characteristics/avg-unemp-rate-1.xlsx", overwrite = TRUE)

```

**Significant Comparisons and Interpretation of "Diff"**

    -   Regional workers came from counties with unemployment rates 0.2 points lower than those in meaningful employment outside the region.
    -   Interpretation: Students from stronger economies were more likely to remain employed within their region rather than seek opportunities elsewhere in Minnesota.
-   **Other comparisons** (e.g., Not meaningful employment vs. others) were not significant, showing that non-meaningful work occurred under similar county unemployment conditions.

### `avg.wages.pct.state`

**Key Findings**\
County wages (as a percent of state wages) show a consistent, statistically significant relationship with outcomes across all three years, though the effect weakens over time (F=14.5 → 16.3 → 6.5). Students with meaningful regional employment consistently came from counties with slightly higher relative wages compared to those working meaningfully outside the region, disconnected, or in non-meaningful jobs. Even small differences (0.6–1.0 percentage points) in local wages shaped whether students stayed in their home region for meaningful work.

**Interpretation Over Time**

-   **Year 1:** Regional workers came from counties with wages about 1 percentage point higher than peers employed meaningfully outside the region. Stronger wage environments encouraged students to remain in their region for quality jobs.\
-   **Year 5:** The pattern persisted. Regional workers had wage advantages of about 1 percentage point over peers meaningfully employed elsewhere in Minnesota, reinforcing the role of local wages in retaining workers.\
-   **Year 10:** Wage effects narrowed but remained significant. Regional workers came from counties with wages about 0.6–0.8 percentage points higher than peers disconnected, in non-meaningful jobs, or employed outside the region.

**Conclusion**\
County wages are a steady High School Characteristic predictor of meaningful regional employment. Although the differences are small in absolute terms, they consistently tilt outcomes toward remaining in the region for meaningful work. Stronger local wage environments both reduce workforce detachment and improve the likelihood of securing meaningful employment in the region.

::: panel-tabset

## High school accomplishments

**Key Findings**\
High School Accomplishments showed clear and consistent relationships with employment outcomes for non-college graduates, though the type and strength of predictors varied:

1.  **ACT-related measures** were among the strongest predictors:

    -   **ACT Taken** (V=0.225 → 0.113 → 0.115) stood out as the single strongest categorical accomplishment variable, sharply dividing college-prep from workforce pathways.\
    -   **ACT Composite Score** (F=28.9 → 39.1 → 57.7) was the strongest continuous test score predictor, with higher scores tied to meaningful employment outside the region and lower scores tied to disconnection and non-meaningful work.

2.  **PSEO Participation** (V=0.135 → 0.052 → 0.081) mattered most in Year 1, increasing likelihood of postsecondary attendance but reducing early regional employment. Its predictive power weakened over time.

3.  **CTE Achievement** showed moderate effects (V≈0.06 across years): concentrators/completors were more likely to be in meaningful regional employment, while students with no CTE were more likely to be disconnected or in non-meaningful jobs. **Total CTE Courses Taken** (F=\~6–20 range) reinforced this, with more courses linked to regional meaningful employment and fewer tied to detachment.

4.  **MCA Scores (Math, Reading, Science)** were consistent but modest predictors (F≈16–50 across years). Higher scores reduced risks of disconnection and non-meaningful work but also increased likelihood of leaving the region for meaningful employment. Lower scores anchored students locally but with weaker job quality and higher detachment risks.

**Interpretation Over Time**

-   **Year 1:** ACT and PSEO most strongly shaped pathways into postsecondary versus early workforce entry. CTE and MCA scores mainly separated students at risk of disconnection from those pursuing education or employment.
-   **Year 5:** ACT and MCA scores became stronger predictors of meaningful statewide employment. CTE continued to support regional employment, while PSEO’s influence weakened.
-   **Year 10:** ACT and MCA scores most sharply distinguished job quality and geography—higher scorers were more likely to leave the region for meaningful work, while lower scorers remained tied to the regional economy with greater vulnerability to non-meaningful jobs or disconnection. CTE maintained a stabilizing effect for regional attachment.

**Conclusion**\
High School Accomplishments strongly predict both the **quality** and **geography** of employment outcomes. Academic measures (ACT, MCA) expanded opportunities but often steered students away from the region, while applied pathways (CTE) promoted regional attachment but did not eliminate risks of lower-quality jobs. Together, these findings highlight a tension: stronger academic preparation helps secure meaningful employment but often outside the region, while CTE fosters local workforce ties but with more mixed long-term outcomes.

<br>

### `pseo.participant`

**Key Findings**\
PSEO participation is significantly related to outcomes across all three years, with effect sizes ranging from small-to-moderate early (Cramer’s V=0.135 at Year 1) to weaker by Years 5 and 10 (V≈0.05–0.08). The clearest distinction is that PSEO participants are more likely to pursue postsecondary education in the short term and later secure meaningful employment outside the region, while non-participants face higher rates of workforce disconnection. However, meaningful regional employment rates remain nearly identical between participants and non-participants across all years.

**Interpretation Over Time**

-   **Year 1:** PSEO participants were far more likely to be attending postsecondary (24.2% vs. 14.5%), less likely to be disconnected (15.7% vs. 23.1%), but also slightly less likely to be in meaningful regional employment (18.8% vs. 20.3%).\
-   **Year 5:** Differences narrowed. Meaningful regional employment was nearly identical (26.4% vs. 26.6%), but PSEO participants were more likely to hold meaningful jobs outside the region (15.1% vs. 11.7%).\
-   **Year 10:** Patterns solidified. Meaningful regional employment remained virtually equal (25.3% vs. 24.8%). PSEO participants continued to be more likely to hold meaningful employment outside the region (20.1% vs. 14.0%) and less likely to be disconnected (35.2% vs. 38.9%).

**Conclusion**\
PSEO participation does not increase the likelihood of meaningful regional employment but does expand opportunities beyond the region. While PSEO helps reduce disconnection and support meaningful employment overall, it channels students more often into jobs outside their home region, suggesting its benefits may contribute more to statewide mobility than regional workforce attachment.

::: panel-tabset
#### 1-year after graduation

**Key Takeaways (Year 1, PSEO Participation)**\
PSEO participation is significantly related to outcomes (χ²=338.5, p\<.001) with a small-to-moderate effect (Cramer’s V=0.135). PSEO participants were more likely to still be attending postsecondary (24.2% vs. 14.5%) and slightly less likely to be in meaningful regional employment (18.8% vs. 20.3%). Non-participants were more often disconnected (23.1% vs. 15.7%), suggesting that PSEO reduced early workforce detachment even if it did not strongly increase meaningful regional employment in the first year.

```{r}

  filter(grad.year.1 != "After 2023") %>%
  filter(ps.grad == "No")

tab_xtab(var.row = data$grad.year.1,
         var.col = data$pseo.participant,
         show.exp = TRUE,
         show.col.prc = TRUE)

```

#### 5-years after graduation

**Key Takeaways (Year 5, PSEO Participation)**\
PSEO participation remains significantly related to outcomes (χ²=33.9, p\<.001) though the effect is weak (Cramer’s V=0.052). By Year 5, PSEO participants were more likely to achieve meaningful employment outside the region (15.1% vs. 11.7%), while rates of meaningful regional employment were nearly identical (26.4% vs. 26.6%). Non-participants were slightly more likely to be disconnected (30.7% vs. 28.1%). This suggests PSEO primarily influenced pathways beyond the region rather than strengthening attachment to meaningful regional jobs.

```{r}

         show.col.prc = TRUE)
```

#### 10-years after graduation

**Key Takeaways (Year 10, PSEO Participation)**\
PSEO participation continues to show a significant relationship with outcomes (χ²=32.7, p\<.001) with a small effect (Cramer’s V=0.081). By Year 10, PSEO participants were more likely to be meaningfully employed outside the region (20.1% vs. 14.0%), while rates of meaningful regional employment were nearly identical (25.3% vs. 24.8%). Non-participants were somewhat more likely to be disconnected (38.9% vs. 35.2%). This indicates that PSEO participation primarily increased opportunities for meaningful work outside the region rather than boosting meaningful regional employment in the long term.

### `cte.achievement`

**Key Findings**\
CTE achievement is consistently related to outcomes for non-college graduates, with weak but stable effects across all years (Cramer’s V ≈ 0.06). The relative outcomes are clear: CTE concentrators/completers achieve the highest rates of meaningful regional employment, CTE participants fall in the middle, and students with no CTE experience the lowest regional employment and highest disconnection.

**Interpretation Over Time**

-   **Year 1:** CTE concentrators/completers had the highest meaningful regional employment (22.9%) compared to participants (19.0%) and no CTE (16.2%). Students with no CTE were more often disconnected (23.4% vs. 19%).\
-   **Year 5:** The gap widened. Regional employment reached 30.2% for concentrators/completers, 27.2% for participants, and 23.0% for no CTE. Disconnection was again highest for no CTE (32.9%).\
-   **Year 10:** The pattern persisted. Regional employment remained strongest among concentrators/completers (29.7%), followed by participants (26.1%), and lowest for no CTE (21.7%). Students with no CTE were most likely to be disconnected (40.5%).

**Conclusion**\
CTE achievement is a consistent High School Accomplishment predictor of meaningful regional employment. While the effect size is modest, the pattern is clear and enduring: deeper CTE engagement increases the likelihood of securing meaningful regional jobs and lowers the risk of long-term workforce detachment. Students with no CTE face persistent disadvantages, with both lower regional employment and higher disconnection.

::: panel-tabset

CTE achievement is significantly related to outcomes (χ²=195.3, p\<.001) with a weak effect (Cramer’s V=0.064). Students who were CTE concentrators or completers had the highest rates of meaningful regional employment (22.9%) compared to CTE participants (19.0%) and students with no CTE (16.2%). Those with no CTE were more likely to be disconnected (23.4% vs. 19–19.4%). This suggests that deeper CTE engagement provides an early advantage in accessing meaningful regional employment and reduces the risk of detachment from the workforce.

### `total.cte.courses.taken`

**Key Findings**\
The total number of CTE courses taken is consistently related to outcomes for non-college graduates, with strong significance across all three years (F=64.4 → 30.5 → 16.5). Effect sizes weaken over time, but the pattern remains clear: students who take more CTE courses are more likely to secure meaningful regional employment, while those who take fewer are more often disconnected or in non-meaningful jobs.

**Interpretation Over Time**

-   **Year 1:** Regional workers had taken about 0.7 more CTE courses than students still in postsecondary, and about 0.5 more than disconnected peers. CTE exposure strongly supported immediate entry into meaningful work.\
-   **Year 5:** The advantage persisted. Regional workers had taken about 0.6 more CTE courses than postsecondary students and about 0.2 more than peers employed meaningfully elsewhere in Minnesota, reinforcing CTE’s role in sustaining regional pathways.\
-   **Year 10:** Effects narrowed but remained significant. Regional workers had taken about 0.4 more CTE courses than disconnected students and about 0.2 more than those in non-meaningful jobs, showing long-term benefits of stronger CTE engagement.

**Conclusion**\
Total CTE course-taking is one of the most consistent High School Accomplishment predictors of meaningful regional employment. While differences shrink over time, greater CTE exposure reliably improves the likelihood of entering and remaining in meaningful regional jobs, and lowers the risk of disconnection or non-meaningful work.

::: panel-tabset
#### 1-year after graduation

**Key Takeaways (Year 1, Total CTE Courses Taken)**\
The total number of CTE courses taken is strongly related to outcomes (F=64.4, p\<.001). Students in meaningful employment—both in the region and elsewhere in Minnesota—completed significantly more CTE courses on average than students attending postsecondary or working in non-meaningful jobs. This suggests that greater CTE exposure provided a direct early advantage for entering meaningful employment.

**Significant Comparisons and Interpretation of "Diff"**

-   **Meaningful employment MN vs. Attending PS**
    -   Diff = **+0.72**, p \< .001
    -   Students in meaningful Minnesota employment had taken, on average, 0.7 more CTE courses than those still attending postsecondary.
    -   Interpretation: Greater CTE exposure nudged students toward early employment instead of continued schooling.
-   **Meaningful regional employment vs. Attending PS**
    -   Diff = **+0.69**, p \< .001
    -   Regional workers had taken about 0.7 more CTE courses than postsecondary students.
    -   Interpretation: Stronger CTE engagement supported entry into regional jobs directly after high school.
-   **Not meaningful employment vs. Attending PS**
    -   Diff = **+0.24**, p \< .001
    -   Students in non-meaningful jobs had taken about 0.2 more CTE courses than those still in school.
    -   Interpretation: CTE exposure increased the likelihood of entering work, though not always in meaningful jobs.
-   **Other comparisons** (e.g., meaningful regional vs. meaningful MN, or disconnection vs. attending PS) were not significant, suggesting CTE course-taking mainly distinguished between employment vs. schooling rather than between employment types.

### `ACTCompositeScore`

**Key Findings**\
ACT composite score shows a consistent, statistically significant relationship with outcomes across all three years (F=50.2 → 28.3 → 17.6). Higher ACT scores are linked to continued postsecondary education and reduced likelihood of immediate workforce entry, while lower scores are associated with earlier employment—especially within the region. Over time, ACT scores also help distinguish job quality, with lower scorers more likely in non-meaningful work and higher scorers more likely disconnected due to educational pursuits.

**Interpretation Over Time**

-   **Year 1:** Regional workers scored nearly 2 points lower than postsecondary students, while statewide meaningful workers scored about 1.3 points lower. Higher ACT performance funneled students into continued schooling, while lower scorers were more likely to work, particularly in their home region.\
-   **Year 5:** Regional workers again scored about 1.7 points lower than postsecondary students and about 1 point lower than peers in meaningful jobs elsewhere in Minnesota. Non-meaningful workers also scored lower, showing ACT differences shaped whether students pursued higher education, meaningful regional work, or low-quality jobs.\
-   **Year 10:** Regional workers scored about 1.2 points lower than peers in meaningful employment elsewhere in Minnesota, while non-meaningful workers scored 1.3 points lower than regional peers. Disconnected students scored about 1 point higher than regional workers, reflecting higher ACT students who did not remain tied to local employment.

**Conclusion**\
ACT composite score is a strong High School Accomplishment predictor in the short term, shaping whether students continue schooling or enter the workforce. Over time, its influence shifts: lower scorers remain more likely in meaningful regional jobs, while higher scorers are more often disconnected or in statewide employment. Ultimately, ACT performance reflects a tradeoff between academic pathways and regional workforce attachment, with lower scores favoring regional retention but not always ensuring job quality.

::: panel-tabset
#### 1-year after graduation

**Key Takeaways (Year 1, ACT Composite Score)**\
ACT composite score is strongly related to outcomes (F=50.2, p\<.001). Students in meaningful employment (both in the region and elsewhere in Minnesota) had significantly lower ACT scores on average than those attending postsecondary. This suggests that higher ACT performance channeled students toward continued schooling, while lower ACT performance was associated with earlier entry into the workforce.

**Significant Comparisons and Interpretation of "Diff"**

-   **Meaningful employment MN vs. Attending PS**
    -   Diff = **-1.26**, p \< .001
    -   Students in meaningful employment elsewhere in Minnesota scored about 1.3 points lower on the ACT than those attending postsecondary.
    -   Interpretation: Higher ACT scores encouraged extended schooling rather than workforce entry.
-   **Meaningful regional employment vs. Attending PS**
    -   Diff = **-1.94**, p \< .001
    -   Regional workers scored nearly 2 points lower on the ACT than postsecondary students.
    -   Interpretation: Students with lower ACT scores were more likely to transition directly into regional employment.
-   **Not meaningful employment vs. Attending PS**
    -   Diff = **-0.66**, p \< .001
    -   Students in non-meaningful jobs scored about two-thirds of a point lower on the ACT than postsecondary students.
    -   Interpretation: Lower ACT performance also increased likelihood of entering low-quality work.
-   **Meaningful regional employment vs. Meaningful employment MN**
    -   Diff = **-0.68**, p = .035
    -   Regional workers scored about 0.7 points lower on the ACT than those in meaningful jobs elsewhere in Minnesota.
    -   Interpretation: Students with somewhat lower ACT scores were more likely to stay in their region for employment.
-   **Other comparisons** (e.g., disconnection vs. others) were not significant, suggesting ACT performance mainly distinguished postsecondary pathways from employment, and regional from statewide work.

### `took.ACT`

**Key Findings**\
ACT participation is one of the stronger High School Accomplishment predictors, with effect sizes ranging from moderate in the short term (Cramer’s V=0.225 at Year 1) to weaker but still significant over time (V≈0.11 at Years 5 and 10). The clearest distinction is that ACT takers are more likely to pursue postsecondary education early on and, by Years 5 and 10, are more likely to achieve meaningful employment outside the region. Non-takers are more likely to enter the regional labor market immediately but face persistently higher risks of disconnection and non-meaningful work.

**Interpretation Over Time**

-   **Year 1:** ACT takers were much more likely to be in postsecondary (29% vs. 13%), while non-takers were more likely in meaningful regional jobs (20.4% vs. 17.3%) or disconnected (25.9% vs. 13.4%).\
-   **Year 5:** ACT takers had higher rates of meaningful employment outside the region (15.7% vs. 10.4%) and slightly higher meaningful regional employment (27.2% vs. 25.6%). Non-takers were more likely disconnected (32.5% vs. 25.7%).\
-   **Year 10:** ACT takers were again more likely in meaningful jobs outside the region (21.0% vs. 12.8%), while meaningful regional employment was identical (25.6% vs. 25.5%). Non-takers remained more likely disconnected (37.7% vs. 34.8%) or in non-meaningful jobs (24.0% vs. 18.6%).

**Conclusion**\
ACT participation clearly distinguishes college-prep and workforce pathways. While it does not increase meaningful regional employment, it expands opportunities for meaningful work elsewhere in Minnesota and lowers the likelihood of disconnection or low-quality employment. Non-takers are more likely to remain tied to the regional workforce, but with greater risks of disconnection and weaker job quality.

::: panel-tabset
#### 1-year after graduation

**Key Takeaways (Year 1, ACT Taken or Not)**\
Whether a student took the ACT is strongly related to outcomes (χ²=1201.7, p\<.001) with a moderate effect size (Cramer’s V=0.225). Students who took the ACT were far more likely to still be attending postsecondary in Year 1 (29% vs. 13%), while those who did not take the ACT were more likely to be in meaningful regional employment (20.4% vs. 17.3%) or disconnected (25.9% vs. 13.4%). This shows that ACT participation strongly segmented students into college-prep versus workforce pathways, with non-takers entering the regional labor market earlier but also facing higher risks of disconnection.

```{r}
data <- master.original %>%
  filter(grad.year.1 != "After 2023") %>%
  filter(ps.grad == "No")

tab_xtab(var.row = data$grad.year.1,
         var.col = data$took.ACT,
         show.exp = TRUE,
         show.col.prc = TRUE)

```

#### 5-years after graduation

**Key Takeaways (Year 5, ACT Taken or Not)**\
ACT participation remains significantly related to outcomes (χ²=222.5, p\<.001) though the effect size weakens (Cramer’s V=0.113). By Year 5, students who had taken the ACT were more likely to be in meaningful employment outside the region (15.7% vs. 10.4%) and slightly more likely to be in meaningful regional jobs (27.2% vs. 25.6%). Non-takers, however, were much more likely to be disconnected (32.5% vs. 25.7%). This suggests that ACT takers were better positioned for both regional and statewide meaningful employment, while non-takers faced higher risks of detachment from the workforce.

```{r}
data <- master.original %>%
  filter(grad.year.5 != "After 2023") %>%
  filter(ps.grad == "No")

tab_xtab(var.row = data$grad.year.5,
         var.col = data$took.ACT,
         show.exp = TRUE,
         show.col.prc = TRUE)

```

#### 10-years after graduation

**Key Takeaways (Year 10, ACT Taken or Not)**\
ACT participation continues to show a significant relationship with outcomes (χ²=133.4, p\<.001) with a weak effect (Cramer’s V=0.115). By Year 10, ACT takers were far more likely to achieve meaningful employment outside the region (21.0% vs. 12.8%), while meaningful regional employment rates were nearly identical (25.6% vs. 25.5%). Non-takers were more likely to be disconnected (37.7% vs. 34.8%) or in non-meaningful jobs (24.0% vs. 18.6%). This shows that taking the ACT expanded opportunities—particularly beyond the region—while not taking it increased long-term risks of detachment and low-quality employment.


### `MCA.M`

**Key Findings**\
MCA Math scores are consistently related to outcomes across all three years (F=16.7 → 16.6 → 31.5). While the effect sizes are modest, math proficiency consistently distinguished disconnected and non-meaningful outcomes from stronger pathways. Over time, MCA Math became more important in differentiating job quality and whether meaningful work occurred within or outside the region.

**Interpretation Over Time**

-   **Year 1:** Disconnected students scored about 0.17 points lower than postsecondary students. Math proficiency primarily distinguished those at risk of workforce detachment from students pursuing education or employment.\
-   **Year 5:** Students in meaningful statewide employment scored about 0.13 points higher than postsecondary peers, while regional workers scored 0.14 points lower than statewide peers. Stronger math skills nudged students toward meaningful employment outside their region rather than regional work.\
-   **Year 10:** Gaps widened. Regional workers scored 0.20 points lower than statewide peers, disconnected students 0.15 points lower, and non-meaningful workers 0.34 points lower than statewide peers. Math proficiency clearly distinguished both job quality and the likelihood of leaving the region for meaningful employment.

**Conclusion**\
MCA Math is a steady predictor of long-term outcomes for non-college graduates. Stronger scores reduce the risk of disconnection and low-quality jobs but also increase the likelihood of leaving the region for meaningful employment. Conversely, lower scores are associated with staying in the region but with greater vulnerability to disconnection or non-meaningful work. Thus, math proficiency shapes both the quality and geography of workforce pathways over time.

::: panel-tabset
#### 1-year after graduating

**Key Takeaways (Year 1, MCA Math Scores)**\
MCA Math scores are significantly related to outcomes (F=16.7, p\<.001). Students with no Minnesota employment record had notably lower math scores than peers attending postsecondary, while differences between meaningful regional employment, meaningful statewide employment, and schooling were smaller. This suggests that math proficiency primarily distinguished students who disconnected from the workforce rather than separating those who entered different types of employment.

**Significant Comparisons and Interpretation of "Diff"**

-   **No MN employment record vs. Attending PS**
    -   Diff = **-0.17**, p \< .001
    -   Disconnected students scored about 0.17 points lower on the MCA Math scale than postsecondary students.
    -   Interpretation: Stronger math skills reduced early risk of workforce detachment.
-   **Other comparisons** (e.g., regional vs. attending PS, or meaningful vs. not meaningful work) were not significant after adjustment, indicating that math scores had limited ability to differentiate employment quality or regional attachment in the first year.

```{r}
data <- master.original %>%
  filter(grad.year.1 != "After 2023") %>%
  filter(ps.grad == "No")

summary <- aov(MCA.M ~ grad.year.1, data = data)

summary

anova_df <- broom::tidy(summary)

TukeyHSD(summary)

tukey_df <- broom::tidy(TukeyHSD(summary))

wb <- createWorkbook()
addWorksheet(wb, "ANOVA")
addWorksheet(wb, "TukeyHSD")
writeData(wb, "ANOVA", anova_df)
writeData(wb, "TukeyHSD", tukey_df)
saveWorkbook(wb, "Data/ChatGPT/Non-college grads/High school accomplishments/MCA-M-1.xlsx", overwrite = TRUE)

```

#### 5-years after graduation

**Key Takeaways (Year 5, MCA Math Scores)**\
MCA Math scores remain significantly related to outcomes (F=16.6, p\<.001). Students in meaningful employment outside the region had slightly higher math scores than peers still attending postsecondary, while regional workers scored lower than their statewide peers. This suggests math proficiency helped distinguish pathways into statewide employment but was less influential for regional employment.

**Significant Comparisons and Interpretation of "Diff"**

-   **Meaningful employment MN vs. Attending PS**
    -   Diff = **+0.13**, p = .032
    -   Students in meaningful statewide employment scored about 0.13 points higher than those still in postsecondary.
    -   Interpretation: Stronger math skills supported transition into statewide employment rather than extended schooling.
-   **Meaningful regional employment vs. Meaningful employment MN**
    -   Diff = **-0.14**, p \< .001
    -   Regional workers scored about 0.14 points lower than peers in meaningful statewide employment.
    -   Interpretation: Students with stronger math skills were more likely to work outside their home region rather than stay local.
-   **Other comparisons** (e.g., disconnection vs. postsecondary, or non-meaningful vs. postsecondary) were not significant, showing that math scores mainly separated regional vs. statewide meaningful employment by Year 5.

```{r}
summary

TukeyHSD(summary)

tukey_df <- broom::tidy(TukeyHSD(summary))

addWorksheet(wb, "ANOVA")
addWorksheet(wb, "TukeyHSD")
writeData(wb, "ANOVA", anova_df)
writeData(wb, "TukeyHSD", tukey_df)
```

#### 10-years after graduation

**Key Takeaways (Year 10, MCA Math Scores)**\
MCA Math scores remain significantly related to outcomes (F=31.5, p\<.001). Students in meaningful regional employment had lower scores than peers in meaningful statewide jobs, while those in non-meaningful jobs had the lowest scores overall. This shows that math proficiency increasingly distinguished job quality and regional vs. statewide employment pathways in the long term.

**Significant Comparisons and Interpretation of "Diff"**

-   **Meaningful regional employment vs. Meaningful employment MN**
    -   Diff = **-0.20**, p \< .001
    -   Regional workers scored about 0.2 points lower than peers in meaningful statewide employment.
    -   Interpretation: Stronger math skills were associated with leaving the region for meaningful jobs elsewhere.
-   **No MN employment record vs. Meaningful employment MN**
    -   Diff = **-0.15**, p \< .001
    -   Disconnected students scored about 0.15 points lower than peers working meaningfully elsewhere in Minnesota.
    -   Interpretation: Higher math skills reduced long-term risk of disconnection.
-   **Not meaningful employment vs. Meaningful employment MN**
    -   Diff = **-0.34**, p \< .001
    -   Students in non-meaningful jobs scored about a third of a point lower than those in meaningful statewide employment.
    -   Interpretation: Math proficiency separated higher-quality jobs from low-quality ones a decade after high school.
-   **Not meaningful employment vs. Meaningful regional employment**
    -   Diff = **-0.14**, p \< .001
    -   Students in non-meaningful jobs scored about 0.14 points lower than regional workers.
    -   Interpretation: Even within the region, stronger math skills supported access to more meaningful employment.
-   **Other comparisons** (e.g., disconnection vs. regional) were not significant, showing that math scores mainly distinguished meaningful statewide jobs and job quality overall.

### `MCA.R`

**Key Findings**\
MCA Reading scores are consistently and significantly related to outcomes across all three years (F=49.8 → 16.7 → 34.7). Reading proficiency shows a clear pattern: higher scores are tied to extended schooling and meaningful work outside the region, while lower scores are associated with earlier regional employment, disconnection, or non-meaningful work.

**Interpretation Over Time**

-   **Year 1:** Students entering meaningful employment (regional or statewide), disconnected students, and those in non-meaningful jobs all scored lower than postsecondary peers (gaps of 0.13–0.29 points). Reading proficiency mainly separated continued education from workforce entry or detachment.\
-   **Year 5:** Regional workers scored about 0.17 points lower than postsecondary students and 0.14 points lower than statewide peers. Disconnected and non-meaningful workers also scored lower than postsecondary peers, showing that stronger reading skills encouraged staying in school or leaving the region for better opportunities.\
-   **Year 10:** Gaps sharpened. Regional workers scored 0.23 points lower than statewide peers, non-meaningful workers scored 0.31 points lower, and disconnected students scored 0.11 points lower than statewide peers. Reading proficiency increasingly distinguished job quality and geography—pushing stronger readers toward meaningful work outside the region.

**Conclusion**\
MCA Reading scores are a durable High School Accomplishment predictor. Higher reading proficiency reduces risk of low-quality or disconnected outcomes but also increases the likelihood of leaving the region for meaningful employment. Lower proficiency anchors students more to the regional labor market but with higher vulnerability to disconnection and weaker job quality.

::: panel-tabset
#### 1-year after graduating

**Key Takeaways (Year 1, MCA Reading Scores)**\
MCA Reading scores are strongly related to outcomes (F=49.8, p\<.001). Students in meaningful employment (regional or statewide) and those disconnected or in non-meaningful work all had lower reading scores than peers attending postsecondary. This shows that reading proficiency primarily distinguished students who continued schooling from those who entered the workforce or disconnected.

**Significant Comparisons and Interpretation of "Diff"**

-   **Meaningful employment MN vs. Attending PS**
    -   Diff = **-0.13**, p \< .001
    -   Students in meaningful statewide jobs scored about 0.13 points lower than those still attending postsecondary.
    -   Interpretation: Higher reading scores encouraged continued schooling rather than workforce entry.
-   **Meaningful regional employment vs. Attending PS**
    -   Diff = **-0.18**, p \< .001
    -   Regional workers scored about 0.18 points lower than postsecondary students.

-   **No MN employment record vs. Attending PS**
    -   Diff = **-0.29**, p \< .001
    -   Disconnected students scored nearly 0.3 points lower than postsecondary students.
    -   Interpretation: Weak reading skills increased risk of workforce detachment.
-   **Not meaningful employment vs. Attending PS**
    -   Diff = **-0.17**, p \< .001
    -   Students in non-meaningful jobs scored about 0.17 points lower than postsecondary peers.
    -   Interpretation: Lower reading scores also increased entry into low-quality jobs.
-   **Other comparisons** (e.g., regional vs. statewide meaningful employment) were not significant, indicating that reading scores mainly separated schooling from employment/disconnection, rather than distinguishing between job types.

### `MCA.S`

**Key Findings**\
MCA Science scores are consistently and significantly related to outcomes across all three years (F=22.5 → 16.7 → 23.2). Disconnected students scored 0.12 points higher than regional workers, suggesting that some high-science scorers pursued opportunities outside the local labor market.

**Conclusion**\
MCA Science scores are a durable High School Accomplishment predictor. Higher science proficiency reduces the risk of low-quality or disconnected outcomes but also increases the likelihood of leaving the region for meaningful employment. Lower science scores anchor students more to the regional workforce, but with greater vulnerability to disconnection and weaker job quality.
